newsitem.title: USA: Martin Luther King autobiography announced.
newsitem.headline: Martin Luther King autobiography announced.

text.p: Plans are afoot to publish Martin Luther King Jr.'s autobiography even though the great civil rights leader never wrote one.

In a unique publishing venture, King's family and Time Warner announced on Wednesday they will assemble his autobiography from the extensive first person references in his speeches, sermons, letters and other writings in order to publish it in 1998 -- the 30th anniversary year of his April 4, 1968, assassination at age 39 in Memphis.

The autobiography will be the centerpiece of a project that will include his widow Coretta Scott King's memoirs, a book by their son Dexter, a collection of Dr King's sermons, audio recordings of his speeches, a CD-ROM on his life and a World Wide Web site that will form an electronic center for discussing his accomplishments.

"Today is a great day for the legacy of Martin Luther King Jr. ... It is exciting to feel that Martin's legacy will be disseminated widely throughout the world," Coretta Scott King told a news conference at Time Warner headquarters, attended by the company's chairman Gerald Levin.

While neither Time Warner officials nor the King family would say how much the rights to the works were sold for, Laurence Kirshbaum, the chairman of the media giant's publishing arm, said it was a multi-million dollar deal.
"This is a very exciting project that will take Martin Luther King's legacy into the next century," Kirshbaum said.

Levin said the website project was especially exciting for Time Warner. "Most of what peope know about famous people today they learn from two-hour docu-dramas. But here we have a chance to make available all the material (from Dr King's life) not some popularized format."
Kirshbaum conceded it was very unusual to assemble a person's autobiography from his past writings but said there was no question that the final work would be an "authentic autobiography."

Dr. Clayborne Carson, a Stanford University professor of history and the director of the Martin Luther King Papers Project, said there were extensive first person accounts of King's life and thoughts to be found in his papers, speeches, letters and sermons, including much material that could shed new light on the civil rights struggles of the 1960s.

"There are gaps, however. We are searching for a first person account of what it was like that day in Oslo when he was awarded the Nobel Peace prize and we are working hard to find a letter he wrote about that," he said.
Carson added, "Everything we use will be something that he wrote. There will be editing (to bring the material into a sequential order) and some changing of tenses."
He said the late Malcolm X never lived to read or approve his autobiography, which was ghostwritten by Alex Haley and published after Malcolm's assassination.

As an example of the sort of material that would be used in the autobiography, he showed reporters an unpublished letter by King to a friend in which he called Richard Nixon a moral coward for being afraid to meet with him or call him during the 1960 election campaign.

King, who led the non-violent protests across the South to end legal segregation, received a telephone call from Nixon's opponent, John F. Kennedy, a call that helped Kennedy win many black votes in a very close election.
In the letter King said that after the election, he did meet with Nixon and praised him as a sincere man who thanks to his Quaker background felt no racism.
